question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Abundant
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ample.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Abundant" means existing or available in large quantities; plentiful. (प्रचुर मात्रा में)
◦ Example: The region has an abundant supply of fresh water.

• "Ample" means enough or more than enough; plentiful, which closely matches the meaning of "abundant".
◦ Example: We have ample time to finish the project before the deadline.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Scarce" (दुर्लभ) means insufficient for the demand; not enough, which is the opposite of abundant.

• Option 3: "Barren" (बंजर) means not producing anything; unfruitful, again opposite in sense to abundant.

• Option 4: "Difficult" (कठिन) means hard to do or understand, which is unrelated to quantity and does not match the meaning of "abundant".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Abundant" useful for SSC exams: plentiful, copious, profuse, bountiful, ample.

• Do not confuse "Abundant" with "Redundant" (अनावश्यक, no longer needed) — the two look similar but have very different meanings.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who does not show response to good or bad
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Stoic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Stoic" is one who does not show any response/reaction to good or bad; a person who remains calm and shows no emotion even in pain or pleasure. (सुख-दुख में समभाव रखने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: Despite losing everything in the fire, he remained a stoic and showed no sign of grief.

• The word comes from Stoicism, a school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught indifference to pleasure and pain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Sceptic" (संशयवादी) means one who doubts generally accepted beliefs or claims.

• Option 3: "Cynic" (निंदक) means one who believes that people are motivated only by self-interest; a distruster of human sincerity.

• Option 4: "Phobic" (भयभीत) means one who has an extreme or irrational fear of something.

NOTE

• Other useful one-word substitutes built on similar patterns: Optimist (one who looks at the bright side), Pessimist (one who looks at the dark side), Fatalist (one who believes everything is predetermined), Altruist (one who works for the welfare of others).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
If you want to be a good detective, it helps to have an inquisitive nature.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Disinterested.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inquisitive" means eager to know or learn about things; curious. (जिज्ञासु)
◦ Example: Children are naturally inquisitive about the world around them.

• "Disinterested" (used here in its common sense of not interested; showing no curiosity) is the closest opposite of "inquisitive" among the given options. (उदासीन, अरुचि रखने वाला)
◦ Example: He remained disinterested throughout the meeting and asked no questions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Comprehensive" (व्यापक) means complete and including everything necessary, unrelated in meaning to "inquisitive".

• Option 2: "Itemised" (मदवार सूचीबद्ध) means listed item by item in detail, unrelated to curiosity.

• Option 3: "Intrusive" (दखल देने वाला) means prying, tending to interfere in others' affairs, which is actually close in meaning to "inquisitive" (a synonym in its negative sense), not its opposite.

NOTE

• In strict formal usage, "disinterested" actually means impartial or unbiased (e.g. a disinterested judge), while "uninterested" means not interested. In competitive exams, however, "disinterested" is frequently tested/accepted in the sense of "uninterested/not curious", as here.

• Other synonyms of "inquisitive": curious, prying, nosy, probing. Other words meaning "indifferent/not curious": apathetic, indifferent, incurious.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The meal was not prepared by us.
option_1: We had not prepare the meal.
option_2: We did not prepare the meal.
option_3: We did not preparing the meal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. We did not prepare the meal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The meal was not prepared by us" is a negative sentence in the Simple Past Tense, Passive Voice.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active (negative): Subject + did not + V1 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "us" becomes the subject "we"; the passive marker "was not" is replaced by "did not"; the past participle "prepared" returns to its base form "prepare"; the object "the meal" stays as the object.
◦ Active: We did not prepare the meal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "We had not prepare" wrongly mixes the Past Perfect auxiliary "had" with the base form "prepare" instead of the past participle, and changes the tense of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "did not preparing" wrongly uses the -ing form after the auxiliary "did"; only the base form of the verb can follow "did" in the Simple Past.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "We did prepare" is an affirmative/emphatic construction, whereas the original sentence is negative in meaning.

NOTE

• In converting passive to active for negative sentences, the auxiliary pattern was/were + not becomes did not (Simple Past) and the main verb reverts from V3 to V1.

• Commonly confused tense markers: Simple Past passive uses "was/were + V3"; Present Perfect passive uses "has/have been + V3"; do not mix the two while converting voice.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The homework must be done by you.
option_1: You should have done the homework.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. You must do the homework.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The homework must be done by you" is written in the Passive Voice with the modal auxiliary "must".

• Rule — Passive with modal "must":
◦ Passive: Object + must + be + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + must + V1 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "you" becomes the subject; the modal "must" is retained as it is; the passive form "be done" becomes the base verb "do"; the object "the homework" stays as the object.
◦ Active: You must do the homework.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "should have done" changes both the modal (must → should) and the aspect of the verb, altering the meaning of obligation expressed in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "You do the homework" drops the modal "must" entirely, removing the sense of obligation/necessity present in the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "You will do the homework" replaces the modal of obligation "must" with the future auxiliary "will", which expresses simple futurity, not necessity.

NOTE

• With modal verbs (must, can, may, should, will, etc.), the modal is retained unchanged when converting between active and passive voice; only the verb form and subject-object positions change.

• Passive of modals: can → can be + V3, may → may be + V3, must → must be + V3, should → should be + V3.

question: Select the correctly spelled sentence.
option_1: I will definitely attend the conference.
option_2: I will definitly attend the conference.
option_3: I will definetely attend the conference.
option_4: I will definately attend the conference.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I will definitely attend the conference.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Definitely" — meaning certainly, without doubt.

• Spelling key: DE + FINITE + LY. The word is built on "finite", so it must contain the letters f-i-n-i-t-e in the middle, followed by the adverb suffix -ly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Definitly" is incorrect because the "e" before the suffix "-ly" (from "finite") has been dropped.

• Option 3: "Definetely" is incorrect because the second "i" in "finite" has wrongly been replaced with "e".

• Option 4: "Definately" is incorrect because it wrongly uses "a" in place of "i" — a very common error since the word is often mispronounced as "definate-ly".

NOTE

• A simple memory trick: "Definitely" contains the word "finite" inside it — if you can spell "finite" correctly, you can spell "definitely" correctly.

• Other commonly misspelled words in SSC exams: separate, occurrence, embarrass, accommodate, questionnaire, rhythm, necessary.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
I would love to organise the farewell party at my house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Arrange.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Organise" means to make arrangements or preparations for an event; to put into a systematic order. (आयोजन करना/व्यवस्थित करना)
◦ Example: The students decided to organise a farewell party for their seniors.

• "Arrange" means to plan or prepare something in advance; to put things in proper order, which matches the meaning of "organise" in this context. (व्यवस्थित करना)
◦ Example: She helped arrange the seating for the guests.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Derange" (अस्तव्यस्त करना) means to throw into disorder; to make insane, which is the opposite of "organise".

• Option 2: "Disorder" (अव्यवस्था) means a state of confusion or lack of order, again opposite to "organise".

• Option 4: "Confuse" (उलझाना) means to mix up or bewilder, unrelated to the sense of planning/arranging.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "organise": arrange, coordinate, plan, systematise, set up.

• Do not confuse "organise" with "organism" (a living being) — the two are unrelated despite similar spelling.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(O) as it was the last one of the evening
(P) the city bus was overcrowded
(Q) and this gave an opportunity
(R) to the pickpockets
(S) to try their skill
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. POQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part (P) "the city bus was overcrowded" introduces the main subject and situation, so it must come first.

• Part (O) "as it was the last one of the evening" gives the reason for the overcrowding, and logically follows immediately after (P).

• Part (Q) "and this gave an opportunity" uses the connector "this" to refer back to the overcrowding described in (P)-(O), so it comes next.

• Parts (R) "to the pickpockets" and (S) "to try their skill" complete the idea of "opportunity" — an opportunity is given "to" someone "to" do something — so R must come before S.

• Reading the full sequence: "The city bus was overcrowded as it was the last one of the evening, and this gave an opportunity to the pickpockets to try their skill." This reads as a complete, logical sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (POQRS).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SRPOQ) is incorrect because it begins with "to try their skill", which cannot logically open the sentence as it lacks a subject.

• Option 2 (PSORQ) is incorrect because placing (S) "to try their skill" immediately after (P) breaks the logical link between "opportunity" and "to try their skill", which must stay together with (Q) and (R).

• Option 4 (SROPQ) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — it starts with (S), which cannot be the opening part of the sentence.

NOTE

• In para/sentence jumble questions, always look for the part that introduces the subject/topic — it is usually the opening part.

• Watch for linking words like "this", "and", "as", "which" — they usually connect to something mentioned just before them and help fix the order.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Every students in the hostel decided to travel to Delhi to witness the Republic Day parade.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Every students in the hostel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The determiner "Every" is always followed by a singular countable noun and a singular verb, never by a plural noun.

• Rule: Every/Each + Singular Noun (+ Singular Verb).

• In the given sentence, "Every students" wrongly pairs the singular determiner "Every" with the plural noun "students". It must be corrected to "Every student".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Republic Day Parade." is correct as it is; it is a proper noun phrase used correctly at the end of the sentence.

• Option 2: "to witness the" is grammatically correct; the infinitive "to witness" correctly expresses purpose.

• Option 3: "decided to travel to Delhi" is correct; "decided" is correctly followed by the infinitive "to travel".

NOTE

• "Every" and "Each" always take a singular noun and singular verb: e.g., "Every student has submitted his project", "Each boy was given a prize."

• Do not confuse this with "All", which is followed by a plural noun: "All students have submitted their projects."

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Break a leg
option_1: Give advice on maintaining physical health.
option_2: Encourage someone to engage in risky activities.
option_3: Suggest taking a short break during work.
option_4: Wish someone good luck before a performance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Wish someone good luck before a performance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Break a leg" means to wish someone good luck, typically before a performance, exam, or important event. (शुभकामनाएं देना, विशेषकर प्रदर्शन से पहले)
◦ Example: Before she walked on stage, her friends told her to break a leg.

• The phrase is traditionally used in theatre, where saying "good luck" directly was considered to invite bad luck, so performers used this indirect expression instead.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To give advice on maintaining physical health is not the meaning of this idiom; it has nothing to do with health advice.

• Option 2: To encourage someone to engage in risky activities is incorrect; the idiom does not literally mean encouraging danger or risk.

• Option 3: To suggest taking a short break during work is incorrect; the idiom is unrelated to taking a rest or pause.

NOTE

• Other common idioms of good wishes/encouragement often asked in SSC: "Fingers crossed" (hoping for a good outcome), "Keep your chin up" (stay positive), "The world is your oyster" (you have every opportunity for success).

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct logical sequence.
A. These can turn around to track stars with the rotation of Earth.
B. Observatories are places to study place.
C. They are mostly built on the mountain tops.
D. Telescopes are placed in the dome-shaped roof of the building.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BCDA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence (B) "Observatories are places to study place" introduces the topic — observatories — so it must be the opening sentence.

• Sentence (C) "They are mostly built on the mountain tops" uses the pronoun "They" to refer back to "Observatories" in (B), so it logically follows (B).

• Sentence (D) "Telescopes are placed in the dome-shaped roof of the building" introduces a new element — telescopes — housed inside the observatory building described in (B)-(C).

• Sentence (A) "These can turn around to track stars with the rotation of Earth" uses the pronoun "These" to refer back to "Telescopes" in (D), so it must come last.

• Reading the sequence: "Observatories are places to study place. They are mostly built on the mountain tops. Telescopes are placed in the dome-shaped roof of the building. These can turn around to track stars with the rotation of Earth." This forms a logically connected passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (BCDA).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (DCBA) is incorrect because it opens with (D), introducing "telescopes" before the topic "observatories" has even been mentioned.

• Option 3 (ACDB) is incorrect because the pronoun "These" in (A) has nothing to refer back to when placed first.

• Option 4 (CBDA) is incorrect because the pronoun "They" in (C) has no antecedent when placed before (B), which is where "Observatories" is first mentioned.

NOTE

• In sentence-ordering questions, always find the sentence that introduces the main subject/topic without using a pronoun — it is almost always the first sentence.

• Track pronouns like "they", "these", "it", "this" carefully — each must logically refer back to a noun already introduced in an earlier sentence.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Abismal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Abysmal" — meaning extremely bad; immeasurably deep.

• Spelling key: AB + Y + SMAL. The word derives from "abyss" (a bottomless chasm), so it retains the letter "y" — a common point where this word is misspelt as "Abismal" with an "i" instead.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Allocation" is correctly spelt — it means the action of distributing resources or duties for a particular purpose.

• Option 3: "Allegation" is correctly spelt — it means a claim or assertion made without proof.

• Option 4: "Aversion" is correctly spelt — it means a strong dislike or unwillingness.

NOTE

• Remember: Abyss → Abysmal (both retain the "y"); this is a useful anchor word to recall the correct spelling.

• Other frequently confused SSC spellings: rhythm, occurrence, embarrass, questionnaire, harass, millennium.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Raju’s job as a clerk seemed to be bad at first because of the low salary, but resulted in something good happening later because it saved him from being unemployed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a blessing in disguise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means something that seems bad or unlucky at first, but turns out to be good in the end. (मुसीबत में भी छिपा वरदान)
◦ Example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise, as it led him to start his own successful business.

• The underlined portion "bad at first because of the low salary, but resulted in something good happening later" exactly describes this idea — something that looked bad initially (low salary) but turned out beneficial later (saved him from being unemployed) — so it can be replaced by this idiom.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a boon in disguise" is not a standard/idiomatic English expression; the fixed idiom uses the word "blessing", not "boon".

• Option 3: "a jolt in disguise" is incorrect; "jolt" means a sudden shock, which does not fit the meaning of something turning out to be good.

• Option 4: "a gift in disguise" is incorrect; this is not a recognised English idiom — the correct fixed form is "a blessing in disguise".

NOTE

• Related idiom of hidden benefit: "Every cloud has a silver lining" (something good can be found in every bad situation).

• Do not alter fixed/idiomatic expressions by substituting synonymous-sounding words (e.g. boon, gift) for the exact word used in the idiom (blessing) — idioms must be reproduced exactly.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(a) the use of animal research
(b) throughout the past century
(c) and it continues to be used to understand many diseases
(d) has been of considerable importance
(e) in the field of scientific and medical advancements
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. adebc.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part (a) "the use of animal research" is the subject of the sentence, so it must come first.

• Part (d) "has been of considerable importance" is the main verb phrase describing the subject, so it directly follows (a).

• Part (e) "in the field of scientific and medical advancements" specifies where this importance applies, following the verb phrase in (d).

• Part (b) "throughout the past century" adds the time frame, completing the first half of the sentence.

• Part (c) "and it continues to be used to understand many diseases" uses the connector "and it" referring back to "animal research" in (a), so it must come last, adding a second clause.

• Reading the sequence: "The use of animal research has been of considerable importance in the field of scientific and medical advancements throughout the past century, and it continues to be used to understand many diseases." This is a coherent, meaningful sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (adebc).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (aecdb) is incorrect because it places (e) directly after (a), breaking the necessary link between the subject (a) and its verb phrase (d).

• Option 2 (ecdba) is incorrect because it opens with (e), which cannot logically begin the sentence without first stating the subject in (a).

• Option 4 (edcba) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 — it wrongly opens with (e) instead of the subject (a).

NOTE

• In sentence-jumble questions, always identify the subject phrase first (usually a noun phrase without a connector) — it almost always opens the sentence.

• Connectors like "and it", "which", "this" typically introduce the concluding part of the sentence, referring back to something already mentioned.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
Spreading awareness about the rights of the consumers and the relief open to them in case they did not get their money’s worth of goods and service has rightly been identified as the first priority.
option_1: were unable to get their money’s worth
option_3: did not getting their money’s worth
option_4: will not get their money’s worth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. were unable to get their money’s worth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "did not get their money's worth" is grammatically acceptable but stylistically weak in this formal context; "were unable to get their money's worth" expresses the same idea in a more precise and formal manner suited to a discussion of consumer rights and relief.

• Rule — Sentence Improvement: when an underlined segment is grammatically correct but can be expressed in a more standard/formal or idiomatic way without changing the meaning, the improved version is preferred over "No substitution".

• "Were unable to get" clearly conveys the sense of inability to obtain fair value, matching the surrounding formal tone of the sentence about consumer rights and relief.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No substitution" is incorrect because a more suitable and formal alternative (Option 1) is available and improves the sentence.

• Option 3: "did not getting their money's worth" is incorrect because the -ing form cannot follow the auxiliary "did"; only the base form of the verb is permitted.

• Option 4: "will not get their money's worth" is incorrect because it wrongly shifts the tense to the future, which does not fit the context of the sentence describing a general/ongoing concern.

NOTE

• In "sentence improvement" questions, always check first whether the underlined portion is grammatically wrong; if it is correct but a better/more idiomatic option exists, choose the improvement rather than "No substitution".

• Common improvement patterns tested by SSC: replacing a plain verb with a more idiomatic phrase (e.g. "did not get" → "were unable to get"), and correcting faulty parallelism or redundancy.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
Pollution levels have increased so largely that they are almost killing us.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. highly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "largely" is normally used to mean "mostly" or "chiefly" (e.g. "largely responsible for"), and does not correctly collocate with "increased" to express a high degree/intensity of increase.

• "Highly" is the correct intensifier used with verbs like "increase" to indicate a great extent or degree — "increased so highly" correctly conveys that pollution levels have gone up to a very great extent.

• Rule — Degree adverbs: words like highly, greatly, considerably, significantly are used to intensify verbs of change (increase, rise, grow), while largely, chiefly, primarily are used to indicate the main cause or extent of responsibility, not degree of increase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "slowly" is incorrect because it describes the speed of an action, and does not fit the meaning of the sentence, which emphasises the harmful extent of the increase, not its pace.

• Option 3: "primarily" is incorrect because it means "mainly/chiefly", which does not correctly modify the degree of an increase.

• Option 4: "chiefly" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3 — it indicates the main reason/cause, not the intensity of increase.

NOTE

• Degree/intensity adverbs commonly tested by SSC: highly, greatly, considerably, significantly, substantially — all correctly used with verbs of change like increase, rise, decline, fall.

• Do not confuse these with adverbs of extent/cause such as largely, mainly, chiefly, primarily, which answer "to what extent/for what main reason", not "by how much".

question:
Identify the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
Scary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. comforting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Scary" means causing fear; frightening. (डरावना)
◦ Example: The old, dark house looked scary at night.

• "Comforting" means giving comfort, consolation, or reassurance; soothing, which is the direct opposite of frightening. (सुखदायक/सांत्वना देने वाला)
◦ Example: Her comforting words calmed the frightened child.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bright" (उज्ज्वल) means giving out light; intelligent, which is unrelated to fear.

• Option 2: "Pristine" (अछूता/निर्मल) means in its original, unspoiled condition, unrelated in meaning to "scary".

• Option 3: "awful" (भयानक) means very bad or unpleasant, and is actually a near-synonym of "scary", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "scary": frightening, terrifying, alarming, spooky, dreadful.

• Other antonyms of "scary"/"frightening": reassuring, soothing, calming, pleasant.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
By this time next year / I will had graduated from college / and starting my first job / in the field of marketing.
option_4: I will had graduated from college
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I will had graduated from college.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "By this time next year" is a marker of the Future Perfect Tense, which describes an action that will be completed before a specified time in the future.

• Rule — Future Perfect Tense: Subject + will have + V3 (past participle).

• The given segment wrongly uses "will had graduated", combining the future auxiliary "will" with the past auxiliary "had", which is grammatically impossible. It must be corrected to "will have graduated".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in the field of marketing" is grammatically correct as a prepositional phrase.

• Option 2: "and starting my first job" is correct here, as it parallels the structure describing future milestones.

• Option 3: "By this time next year" is correct; it is the standard time-marker phrase that signals the Future Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Common time markers for the Future Perfect Tense: "by the time", "by next year", "by 2030", "by then" — all are followed by "will have + V3", never "will had".

• Do not confuse the Future Perfect (will have + V3) with the Past Perfect (had + V3) — mixing "will" and "had" together, as in this question, is a very common SSC error-spotting trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in bold.
Elisabeth stood at the piano, which did nothing to allay his anxiety.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. aggravate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Allay" means to reduce the intensity of a fear, doubt, or worry; to relieve or calm. (शांत करना/कम करना)
◦ Example: The doctor's reassurance helped allay her fears about the surgery.

• "Aggravate" means to make a problem, situation, or feeling worse, which is the direct opposite of "allay". (और बिगाड़ना/बढ़ाना)
◦ Example: His careless remark only aggravated the tension in the room.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "mitigate" (कम करना) means to make something less severe or serious, which is a synonym of "allay", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "simplify" (सरल बनाना) means to make something easier to understand or do, unrelated to calming fear or anxiety.

• Option 3: "mollify" (शांत करना) means to soothe or calm someone's anger/anxiety, which is also a synonym of "allay", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "allay": alleviate, ease, soothe, pacify, assuage.

• Other antonyms of "allay": intensify, worsen, heighten, exacerbate.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Berserk
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Demented.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Berserk" means wildly out of control; in a violent or uncontrollable rage or frenzy. (उन्मत्त/पागलों जैसा)
◦ Example: The bull went berserk when it saw the red flag.

• "Demented" means mad, insane, or behaving in a wild, irrational manner, which closely matches the frenzied, out-of-control sense of "berserk". (उन्मत्त/पागल)
◦ Example: He acted like a demented man after hearing the shocking news.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Absurd" (बेतुका) means wildly unreasonable or illogical, which describes an idea or statement, not a frenzied state of mind.

• Option 3: "Stubborn" (जिद्दी) means refusing to change one's opinion or course of action, unrelated to frenzy or rage.

• Option 4: "Lazy" (आलसी) means unwilling to work or use energy, which is essentially the opposite of the wild, high-energy sense of "berserk".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "berserk": frenzied, crazed, wild, frantic, deranged.

• Common phrase: "to go berserk" — to suddenly become extremely angry or violent.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

From the beginning (1)_________ the eighteenth century, the ladies of European cities covered (2)_______ faces in layers of paint and powder. This particular fashion was largely brought (3) __________ by the urgent need to disguise the ravages of smallpox, (4)_________ left their faces pitted and scarred. During this same period, the ‘beauty spot’ was introduced to cover (5) __________ a facial defect.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "From the beginning of + [a time period]" is a fixed prepositional phrase used to indicate the starting point of a period of time.

• Rule: The preposition "of" is used after nouns like beginning, end, middle to connect them to the time period they refer to — e.g. "at the beginning of the year", "by the end of the month".

• Applying this rule: "From the beginning of the eighteenth century" correctly expresses the starting point of the described period.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in" is incorrect because "in" is not used to connect "beginning" with the time period that follows it.

• Option 2: "on" is incorrect because "on" is used with specific days/dates, not with a phrase like "beginning of a century".

• Option 4: "about" is incorrect because "about" indicates approximation, which does not fit the fixed phrase "beginning of".

NOTE

• Similar fixed prepositional phrases: "at the end of", "in the middle of", "towards the close of" — all followed by "of" before the time period.

• Prepositions with time nouns are frequently tested in SSC cloze passages; learn common noun + preposition combinations like "beginning of", "reason for", "solution to".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

From the beginning (1)_________ the eighteenth century, the ladies of European cities covered (2)_______ faces in layers of paint and powder. This particular fashion was largely brought (3) __________ by the urgent need to disguise the ravages of smallpox, (4)_________ left their faces pitted and scarred. During this same period, the ‘beauty spot’ was introduced to cover (5) __________ a facial defect.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. their.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a possessive adjective to show that the faces being covered belong to "the ladies" mentioned earlier in the same clause.

• Rule: A possessive adjective (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) must agree in number and person with the noun it refers back to. Since "the ladies" is plural (third person), the correct possessive adjective is "their".

• Applying the rule: "the ladies ... covered their faces" correctly shows that the faces belong to the ladies themselves.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "there" is incorrect because it is an adverb of place, not a possessive adjective, and does not fit before the noun "faces".

• Option 3: "them" is incorrect because it is an object pronoun, and cannot be used directly before a noun to show possession.

• Option 4: "they're" is incorrect because it is a contraction of "they are", which does not make sense grammatically before the noun "faces".

NOTE

• Do not confuse the homophones "their" (possessive adjective), "there" (place/existence), and "they're" (they are) — this is a very common SSC trap.

• Possessive adjectives always precede a noun: my book, her bag, their faces, its tail.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

From the beginning (1)_________ the eighteenth century, the ladies of European cities covered (2)_______ faces in layers of paint and powder. This particular fashion was largely brought (3) __________ by the urgent need to disguise the ravages of smallpox, (4)_________ left their faces pitted and scarred. During this same period, the ‘beauty spot’ was introduced to cover (5) __________ a facial defect.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "to bring about" means to cause something to happen.

• Rule — Phrasal verb: "bring" combines with different particles to form different meanings: bring about (to cause), bring up (to raise a child/mention a topic), bring down (to reduce/overthrow), bring in (to introduce).

• Applying the rule: "This particular fashion was largely brought about by the urgent need..." means the fashion was caused/produced by that need — which fits the sense of the sentence perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "within" is incorrect because "brought within" is not a standard collocation with "brought" in this context.

• Option 2: "around" is incorrect because "brought around" means to persuade someone or to help someone regain consciousness, which does not fit here.

• Option 3: "to" is incorrect because "brought to" typically means to bring someone back to consciousness (e.g. "brought to her senses"), not to cause something.

NOTE

• Other useful "bring" phrasal verbs for SSC: bring off (to succeed in doing something difficult), bring out (to reveal/publish), bring forward (to move to an earlier date).

• Always learn phrasal verbs as complete units with their fixed particles — swapping the particle changes the meaning entirely.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

From the beginning (1)_________ the eighteenth century, the ladies of European cities covered (2)_______ faces in layers of paint and powder. This particular fashion was largely brought (3) __________ by the urgent need to disguise the ravages of smallpox, (4)_________ left their faces pitted and scarred. During this same period, the ‘beauty spot’ was introduced to cover (5) __________ a facial defect.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. which.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a relative pronoun to introduce a non-defining relative clause describing "the ravages of smallpox", a thing (not a person).

• Rule: "Which" is the relative pronoun used for things/non-living antecedents, while "who" is used for people and "that" is generally avoided after a comma in a non-defining clause.

• Applying the rule: "...the ravages of smallpox, which left their faces pitted and scarred" correctly uses "which" to refer back to "the ravages of smallpox".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that" is incorrect because "that" is not used to introduce a non-defining relative clause set off by a comma.

• Option 3: "when" is incorrect because "when" is a relative adverb used for time, not for referring to a thing like "ravages".

• Option 4: "who" is incorrect because "who" is used only for people, not for things like "the ravages of smallpox".

NOTE

• Relative pronoun usage: who (person, subject), whom (person, object), which (thing/animal), whose (possession), that (person or thing, only in defining clauses, never after a comma).

• A comma before a relative pronoun always signals a non-defining clause, which cannot use "that".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

From the beginning (1)_________ the eighteenth century, the ladies of European cities covered (2)_______ faces in layers of paint and powder. This particular fashion was largely brought (3) __________ by the urgent need to disguise the ravages of smallpox, (4)_________ left their faces pitted and scarred. During this same period, the ‘beauty spot’ was introduced to cover (5) __________ a facial defect.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "to cover up" means to hide or conceal something, such as a fault, mark, or defect.

• Rule — Phrasal verb: "cover" combines with the particle "up" to specifically mean concealing something from view or notice, which is stronger/more specific than the plain verb "cover".

• Applying the rule: "...the 'beauty spot' was introduced to cover up a facial defect" correctly conveys that the beauty spot was used to conceal/hide a facial flaw.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "on" is incorrect because "cover on" is not a standard English collocation.

• Option 2: "to" is incorrect because "cover to" is not a recognised phrasal verb or standard usage here.

• Option 3: "for" is incorrect because "cover for" means to substitute for someone temporarily (e.g. "cover for a colleague"), which does not fit the meaning of concealing a defect.

NOTE

• Other useful "cover" phrasal verbs for SSC: cover for (substitute for someone), cover up for (protect someone by hiding their fault), cover over (spread over to hide something).

• "Cover up" is frequently used figuratively too: "to cover up a scandal/mistake".
